newsitem.title: FRANCE: President to open France's new national library.
newsitem.headline: President to open France's new national library.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac inaugurates the costly new Francois Mitterrand National Library on Tuesday in a ceremony tinged with irony as Chirac tried to block its construction while mayor of Paris in the early 1990s.

The sleek glass and steel complex built by the late Socialist president cost some 30 billion francs ($6 billion), far above initial projections, and the conservative Chirac tried repeatedly to block or delay it, library officials said.

Mitterrand, who left office in May 1995 and died last January, acknowledged during one of his last interviews as president that he had rushed construction so the complex would be too far along to be torn down when voters threw out France's Socialist government in 1993 general elections.

The project has come under fierce attack from politicians and intellectuals unhappy over its looks and fearful that its operating costs and salaries for 2,700 employees would eat up the national culture budget.
Now that it is about to open, critics may be charmed by its high-tech furnishings and sumptuous woodwork laid next to steel-grey cast concrete walls.
But ecologists say much of the wood comes from endangered Amazonian species and many visitors may be daunted by the fortress-like design by architect Dominique Perrault.

Intended as a homage to recorded knowledge, the complex is curiously folded in on itself, as if purposefully sealed off from its admittedly dreary surroundings, which consist of a maze of railway tracks, roads and public housing by the River Seine.
Once the entrance is located, visitors must pass through a barrier of bushes imprisoned in wire mesh cages before descending into the centre of the complex on a moving sidewalk.
In another odd twist, the inner courtyard is planted with an urban forest of wild pine, birch and elm trees.

Though the library's four L-shaped towers are each 18 stories high, with six more levels below ground, just one of these levels will be open to the general public while a second level will eventually be open to scholars only.
The national library's main collection of 10 million volumes will not be moved into the new complex until 1998 and even then will be kept in rooms accessible only to library workers.
The books will be transferred from the current French national library in the capital's second district at an average rate of 25,000 to 30,000 volumes a day over the next two years.
An admission fee of 20 francs ($4) a day or 200 francs ($40) a year will be charged, and no one under 18 will be admitted without a high school diploma.

The main public rooms will initially offer open access to just 180,000 general reference books and 1,697 seats. In one of many high-tech touches, subsequent visitors will be able to consult computer screens to help find empty seats.
Also to be inaugurated on Tuesday is a tapestry by U.S. pop artist Roy Lichtenstein called "Water Lilies" in a tribute to French painter Claude Monet.

The old national library, located between the Rue de Richelieu and the Rue Vivienne to the north of the Palais Royal, will be renamed after Cardinal de Richelieu, who served as chief minister to King Louis XIII from 1624 until his death in 1642.
It will become France's main depository for the state's collections of manuscripts, engravings, maps, music, coins and theatrical items.
